company_name: Franklin Templeton, Inc. (formerly Franklin Resources, Inc.)
overview: Franklin Templeton is a global investment management holding company offering equity, fixed income, alternative, multi-asset, and cash management solutions to retail, institutional, and high-net-worth clients through a multi-affiliate platform of specialist managers (Franklin, Templeton, ClearBridge, Western Asset, Putnam, Royce, Clarion Partners, Benefit Street Partners, Lexington Partners, and others). The company formally changed its legal name from Franklin Resources, Inc. to Franklin Templeton, Inc. effective August 17, 2026, unifying its corporate identity with its long-standing brand (ticker remains BEN on the NYSE; the change had no effect on capital structure or shareholder rights). As of its fiscal year end September 30, 2026, it managed a record ~$1.795 trillion in AUM across more than 30 countries, with roughly 71% of AUM sold in the U.S. and the remainder internationally (EMEA, Asia-Pacific including India, and the Americas ex-U.S.).

business_model.summary: Franklin Templeton earns investment management fees generally calculated as a percentage of AUM across its multi-affiliate platform, supplemented by sales/distribution fees, shareholder servicing fees, and performance/incentive fees. Fee revenue is therefore directly leveraged to AUM levels, which move with both net client flows and market appreciation/depreciation. The firm has diversified from historically equity/fixed-income mutual funds into higher-fee alternatives (private credit, real estate, PE secondaries), ETFs, retail SMAs/Canvas direct indexing, and digital assets to offset structural fee compression in traditional active mutual funds.

revenue_streams.name: Investment management fees (AUM-based)
revenue_streams.trend: growing (+7% FY2026 to $7.48B; effective fee rate ex-performance fees 40.7bps, up slightly from 40.5bps in FY2025)

revenue_streams.name: Sales and distribution fees
revenue_streams.trend: growing (+8% FY2026 to $1.59B, driven by higher average AUM and mix shift to equity/alternative funds)

business_model.customer_type: Mixed retail (individuals via financial advisors, U.S. and non-U.S. mutual funds) and institutional (pensions, sovereign wealth funds, insurers, endowments, defined contribution plans), plus a growing high-net-worth/private-wealth channel (Fiduciary Trust International) and retail SMA/direct-indexing clients via Canvas
business_model.geographic_mix: AUM by sales region at FY2026 year-end: United States ~71% ($1,272.3B), Europe/Middle East/Africa ~13% ($226.1B), Asia-Pacific (incl. India) ~11% ($191.7B), Americas ex-U.S. ~6% ($105.0B); non-U.S. products generally carry higher fee rates than U.S. products

competitive_position.market_position: One of the more widely diversified U.S.-based global asset managers (~$1.8 trillion AUM), far smaller in scale than passive giants BlackRock and Vanguard, but with deep active-management franchises in global/international equities (Templeton), U.S. equities (ClearBridge, Franklin Equity), fixed income (Western Asset, Franklin Templeton Fixed Income), municipal bonds, and a rapidly scaling alternatives platform (Benefit Street Partners in private credit, Clarion Partners in real estate, Lexington Partners in PE secondaries) that reached a record $304.6 billion AUM (17% of total) in FY2026, among the largest alternatives platforms housed within a traditional long-only manager.

moat_factors.description: Specialist Investment Groups (Western Asset, ClearBridge, Templeton, Royce, Putnam, Clarion, BSP, Lexington) retain investment autonomy and brand identity, aiding talent retention and product breadth across asset classes, vehicles and geographies

Record $304.6 billion alternatives AUM (+$48.7B of FY2026 fundraising) built via acquisitions (Benefit Street Partners 2019, Lexington Partners 2022, Alcentra 2022, Apera 2025) plus the Oct 2026 BSP/Encina asset-backed finance deal and the pending Clarion/Stoneshield real-assets acquisition, giving stickier, higher fees than traditional long-only funds

Long-standing global distribution network across U.S. and international retail/institutional channels, including a substantial India mutual fund franchise (Asia-Pacific AUM $191.7B) and growing insurance/retirement sub-advisory partnerships

79-year operating history; the unified Franklin Templeton brand (name change completed August 2026) and the Templeton global/international and Franklin fixed-income/muni heritage carry recognition with financial advisors
Johnson family (CEO Jennifer Johnson; Executive Chairman Gregory Johnson; Vice Chairman Rupert Johnson Jr.) provides long-term orientation but also governance concentration risk

weaknesses: Structural fee compression in core active equity/fixed income mutual funds from low-cost passive and ETF competition; management itself flags a continued industry-wide shift away from actively managed core equities and fixed income toward alternative, passive and smart-beta strategies
Historical reliance on traditional active mutual funds (39% of AUM measured for performance purposes), a structurally shrinking category relative to ETFs/passive/SMAs

Reputational and flow damage from the Western Asset Management (Ken Leech) trade-allocation scandal; WAM still posted $11.7 billion of long-term net outflows in FY2026 even as redemptions have eased materially from the ~$120B+ pace of FY2025

Complex multi-affiliate structure with 9,900 employees across 30+ countries creates integration friction and redundant cost bases (ongoing office consolidation, e.g. New York City space reduction, and workforce optimization/termination costs in FY2026)
Reliance on third-party broker-dealers, banks and intermediaries for fund distribution, which do not control recommendations and may sell competing or proprietary products
Smaller scale than mega-cap passive competitors limits ability to compete purely on price in commoditized index/ETF products

growth_drivers: Alternatives expansion: record $304.6 billion alternatives AUM with $48.7 billion of FY2026 fundraising; management guides private markets fundraising to a mid-$30 billion range for FY2027
ETF platform scaling to a record $84.6 billion AUM, up 73% year-over-year; management raised its longer-term ETF AUM target to $200 billion (by fiscal 2029)
Canvas custom-indexing/SMA platform, which roughly doubled to $32.6 billion in FY2026, capturing the shift toward personalized, tax-efficient direct indexing
Retail SMA platform at a record $196.3 billion AUM (+19% YoY), benefiting from the broader industry shift from mutual funds to separately managed accounts
Digital assets: the June 2026 acquisition of 250 Digital created the new Franklin Crypto group, expanding tokenized fund offerings and blockchain-based infrastructure (Benji platform)

Continued alternatives M&A: pending majority-stake acquisition of Stoneshield Capital (European real assets, via Clarion Partners, announced Sept 2026, expected to close Q4 calendar 2026) and the October 2026 Benefit Street Partners/Encina Lender Finance asset-backed finance platform deal
Operating leverage: adjusted operating margin expanded 350bps to 28.0% in FY2026; management guides to ~30% in FY2027 and has raised its longer-term target to 35% by fiscal Q4 2029

Broad-based positive net flows: $84.1 billion of long-term net inflows in FY2026 (vs. -$97.4B of total net flows in FY2025), with inflows up 38% and outflows down 12% year-over-year, including a return to positive flows in equity
International/emerging market distribution, including the large India mutual fund franchise and continued EMEA (+12% AUM) and Asia-Pacific (+7% AUM) growth

Strengthened senior leadership bench: Daniel Gamba (formerly BlackRock/iShares and Northern Trust Asset Management) joined as Co-President and Chief Commercial Officer in October 2025, alongside Co-Presidents Terrence Murphy and Matthew Nicholls, broadening executive capacity for the multi-pronged growth strategy

business.description: Revenue depends on the level and mix of AUM; management explicitly flags that a shift toward lower-fee products (fixed income, ETFs) or market declines would reduce fee revenue with limited offsetting cost flexibility

WAM still posted $11.7 billion of long-term net outflows in FY2026; while the pace has eased sharply from the FY2025 peak, the firm settled SEC charges for $100 million in June 2026 over the Ken Leech trade-allocation scandal, and the former co-CIO faces separate criminal proceedings

Company's own risk factors cite a continued industry shift away from actively managed core equities/fixed income toward alternative, passive and smart-beta strategies, pressuring both flows and average fee rates
Heavily reliant on third-party broker-dealers, banks and intermediaries who may recommend or sell competing/proprietary products; rising distribution costs amid channel consolidation

A steady cadence of recent acquisitions (Apera Oct 2025, 250 Digital June 2026, pending Stoneshield) and the BSP/Encina platform deal, alongside ongoing WAM restructuring, create culture and integration risk
Only ~50-55% of mutual fund AUM ranks in the top two peer quartiles over 1/3/5-year periods; sustained underperformance could trigger redemptions

financial.description: Effective investment management fee rate ex-performance fees was roughly flat at 40.7bps in FY2026 (40.5bps FY2025); management guides the adjusted effective fee rate to stay broadly in line with FY2026 levels, signalling limited organic pricing power

Compensation and benefits rose 4% to $3.96 billion in FY2026 on higher incentive pay and termination/workforce-optimization costs; FY2027 guidance of ~$975 million assumes $125 million of performance fees at a 55% payout ratio
Cash management AUM saw $2.8 billion of net outflows in FY2026, a smaller drag than prior periods but still a headwind to the lower-fee segment

$33.0 million of intangible impairment recorded in FY2026 (down from $226.6M in FY2025), reflecting ongoing risk of goodwill/intangible write-downs tied to acquired affiliates if AUM or performance deteriorates

regulatory.description: The WAM $100 million SEC civil penalty (June 2026) for supervisory failures illustrates ongoing regulatory and litigation risk across the multi-affiliate structure; further private litigation tied to the same conduct remains possible

regulatory.risk: Evolving fiduciary, proxy and private-fund disclosure rules
regulatory.description: DOL fiduciary rule reinstatement/QPAM exemption changes, SEC Form PF amendments (compliance extended to July 2027), and proxy-advisory rule changes add compliance complexity and cost

regulatory.risk: Fund Names Rule and sustainability disclosure regimes
regulatory.description: SEC Names Rule amendments and evolving EU SFDR/CSDDD and U.K. Sustainability Disclosure Requirements could require fund renaming, strategy changes or added disclosure costs

Operating across 30+ countries (including a growing digital-asset/crypto business) exposes the firm to a patchwork of securities, tax, GDPR-style privacy, and digital-asset regulations; GDPR non-compliance alone could expose the firm to fines up to 4% of global revenue

macro.description: AUM-linked fee revenue is directly exposed to market drawdowns; FY2026 AUM growth was aided by $126.1 billion of market appreciation, a tailwind that would reverse in a downturn
Fixed income AUM (24% of total, including WAM) is sensitive to rate moves affecting fund performance/flows and cash management yields

Growing private credit book (Benefit Street Partners, newly expanded asset-backed finance platform via Encina) carries direct credit-cycle risk if defaults rise in leveraged loan/private credit markets

A stronger U.S. dollar reduced FY2026 AUM by $4.4 billion via translation versus the Euro, Yen and Indian Rupee (partly offset by a weaker dollar vs. the Australian dollar); non-U.S. AUM generally carries higher fee rates, so FX swings affect both AUM levels and realized fee mix

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global asset management remains large but bifurcating: passive/index and ETF products continue taking share from traditional active mutual funds, while private markets/alternatives are the fastest-growing segment as institutions and increasingly retail/wealth clients seek higher-yielding, less-correlated exposures. Direct indexing/SMAs and digital-asset tokenization are emerging secular growth niches Franklin Templeton is actively targeting (Canvas, Franklin Crypto/Benji).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high -- AUM-based fee revenue is pro-cyclical with equity and credit markets; FY2026 results show how ~$126 billion of market appreciation flowed straight through to AUM and fee revenue, a dynamic that cuts both ways
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate -- affects fixed income fund performance/flows (24% of AUM), cash management yields (4% of AUM), and the credit backdrop for the growing private credit/alternatives book
key_input_costs: Compensation and benefits (largest expense line at $3.96B in FY2026, market-driven for portfolio managers/senior talent)
Sales, distribution and marketing costs paid to financial intermediaries ($2.2B in FY2026, +9%)

recent_developments.event: Reported record fiscal Q4/FY2026 results (Nov 6, 2026): record AUM of $1,795.1 billion (+8% YoY), FY2026 long-term net inflows of $84.1 billion, adjusted EPS of $0.94 in Q4 (vs. $0.78 consensus) and $3.07 for the full year; adjusted operating margin expanded 350bps to 28.0% for FY2026 (31.8% in Q4); shares rose roughly 4-7% on the print

Analysts trimmed/adjusted targets following the print: KBW cut its price target to $37 from $38 (Nov 10, 2026); consensus clustered in the mid-$30s to high-$30s with a Hold/Equal-Weight-leaning rating

Benefit Street Partners completed a transaction with Encina Lender Finance, expanding BSP's asset-backed finance platform via a new fund that acquired an initial ~$480 million seed portfolio; an Encina investment team joined BSP
Entered a definitive agreement for Clarion Partners to acquire a majority stake in Stoneshield Capital, a European real-assets manager, expected to close in Q4 calendar 2026

Corporate name change from Franklin Resources, Inc. to Franklin Templeton, Inc. became effective August 17, 2026 (ticker remains BEN); a legal/branding change only, with no impact on capital structure or shareholder rights

Completed acquisition of 250 Digital, an active cryptocurrency investment manager, forming the new Franklin Crypto group; Western Asset Management separately settled SEC charges tied to the Ken Leech trade-allocation/cherry-picking scandal for a $100 million civil penalty (DOJ declined to pursue the firm; the former co-CIO faces separate criminal proceedings)

Completed the acquisition of Apera Asset Management, a European private credit firm, expanding the alternatives platform; management also named Daniel Gamba (formerly of BlackRock/iShares and Northern Trust Asset Management) Co-President and Chief Commercial Officer alongside Co-Presidents Terrence Murphy and Matthew Nicholls

Fiscal 2025 (ended Sept 30, 2025) revenue of $8.77 billion (+3.5% YoY); AUM declined slightly to $1,661.2 billion as $122.7 billion of fixed-income-driven net outflows (concentrated at WAM) were largely offset by market gains, alongside continued WAM restructuring and job cuts

guidance.fiscal_year: FY2027 (ending September 30, 2027), with longer-term targets through FY2029

items.notes: Would achieve management's original five-year margin goal roughly two years early, following 350bps of expansion to 28.0% in FY2026; assumes flat markets
Raised from a prior longer-term target of approximately 30%
Follows ETF AUM growth of 73% to $84.6 billion in FY2026
FY2026 actual fundraising was $48.7 billion, well above the firm's initial FY2026 target of $25-30 billion
Assumes $125 million of performance fees at a 55% payout ratio

items.target: broadly in line with FY2026 (~40.7bps ex-performance fees)
items.notes: Reflects offsetting effects of higher-fee alternatives/equity growth versus continued fixed income/cash management mix pressure

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Jennifer Johnson highlighted record AUM, broad-based positive net flows across nearly all asset classes, regions and client channels (including equity returning to positive flows), and accelerating momentum in alternatives, ETFs, SMAs/Canvas and digital assets as the core pillars of the growth strategy. Management characterized WAM outflows as continuing to ease rather than fully resolved, with ongoing restructuring and cost actions. The firm sees 'significant opportunities' as the industry evolves toward private markets, customization and innovative vehicles, and framed the August 2026 Franklin Templeton name change as capping a multi-year effort to unify the corporate brand globally.

bull_case: Record AUM (~$1.8 trillion, +8% YoY) and accelerating net inflows ($84.1 billion in FY2026, reversing a net outflow year in FY2025) show the franchise stabilizing and growing despite the WAM overhang

Fast-growing, higher-fee alternatives platform (record $304.6 billion AUM, $48.7 billion of FY2026 fundraising) plus ETFs (+73% to $84.6B), retail SMAs (+19% to $196.3B) and Canvas (roughly doubled to $32.6B) diversify revenue away from commoditized active mutual funds and into secular-growth vehicles
Operating margin expansion is ahead of plan: 28.0% in FY2026 (+350bps), guided to ~30% in FY2027 (hitting a five-year target two years early) and raised to a 35% long-term target by fiscal Q4 2029

WAM-related outflows have eased sharply (from well over $100 billion in prior periods to $11.7 billion in FY2026) alongside a June 2026 SEC settlement that caps the regulatory liability at $100 million, removing a key overhang

Continued disciplined M&A in alternatives (Apera, Stoneshield agreement, BSP/Encina) and a new Franklin Crypto/digital-assets business position the firm to capture both private-markets and tokenization secular trends, supported by a strengthened executive bench (new Co-President/Chief Commercial Officer Daniel Gamba from BlackRock/iShares)
bear_case: Reputational damage from the Western Asset Management trading-allocation scandal persists -- WAM still bled $11.7 billion of long-term net outflows in FY2026, and the $100 million SEC penalty plus ongoing criminal proceedings against the former co-CIO remain overhangs on institutional trust

Structural active-to-passive fee compression is a permanent industry headwind that Franklin Templeton itself identifies as a key risk factor; the adjusted effective fee rate (~40.7bps) is guided to stay flat rather than expand, signaling limited organic pricing power

FY2026 AUM growth was substantially aided by $126.1 billion of market appreciation; a market correction would mechanically reverse both AUM levels and fee revenue, and could reignite redemption pressure across the multi-affiliate platform

Rising compensation and distribution costs (comp +4% to $3.96B, sales/distribution/marketing +9% to $2.2B in FY2026) could offset revenue gains if markets turn down or flows stall, pressuring the ambitious FY2027/FY2029 margin targets

Investment performance is mixed -- only ~50-55% of mutual fund AUM ranks in top-two peer quartiles over 1/3/5-year horizons -- and analyst sentiment remains lukewarm (Hold/Equal-Weight-leaning ratings, price targets clustered in the mid-$30s, with at least one target trimmed in November 2026), suggesting limited market conviction that recent momentum changes the long-term growth trajectory
